messages.content:
Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Depression was associated with increased likelihood of vitamin D deficiency; read with vitamin D as the exposure, lower vitamin D went with more depression.
Sentence: "Diabetes type 2 (HbA1c ≥ 6.5%), depression, and obesity were significantly associated with an increased likelihood of VDD after accounting for other covariates."
Measured as: depression
Population: 216 adults recruited from randomly selected community-based healthcare settings in the UAE
Intervention: None; observational, vitamin D deficiency (serum level ≤ 30 nmol/L)
Comparator: Adults without vitamin D deficiency
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 216
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Serum vitamin D levels showed no significant association with EPDS-defined postpartum depression (EPDS ≥9).
Sentence: "We defined an EPDS score of ≥9 as being positive for postpartum depression, and serum ketone levels were found to be higher in the group with an EPDS score of ≥9 during the second trimester; however, there were no other significant findings."
Measured as: postpartum depression (EPDS score ≥9)
Population: Pregnant women in Japan followed through pregnancy and postpartum (99 analyzed)
Intervention: Serum vitamin D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Women with EPDS <9 vs ≥9
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 126
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are observational and bear on vitamin D and depression, but one finds lower vitamin D linked to depression in a general adult cross-sectional sample while the other finds no association in pregnant women with postpartum depression (EPDS ≥9).","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["outcome_measure","design_or_bias"],"detail":"population: community adults (n=216) vs pregnant/postpartum Japanese women (99 analyzed); depression vs EPDS ≥9 postpartum depression"}
